ch61.essay:
This is the first whale we actually see killed, and Melville makes us wait through a trance to get there. The chapter opens as a lullaby: a vacant sea, three men swaying lifelessly from the spars, the helmsman nodding, and then, in one of the loveliest sentences in the book, the whole world nodding with them, "east nodded to west, and the sun over all." I always feel the book itself falling asleep here, and I think that is the point. The kill comes as a rude awakening, a burgher with a pipe suddenly become a thing bleeding "like brooks down a hill."

What unsettles me most is how the tone refuses to settle. Stubb's patter ("cucumbers is the word") is genuinely funny; the harpoon line blistering through his bare hands is genuinely terrifying; and then the lance is churned into the whale "as if cautiously seeking to feel after some gold watch" — a domestic, almost tender image for the act of finding a heart and bursting it. Melville keeps switching the lights on and off. The sun reflecting off the blood so that every man "glowed to each other like red men" is the chapter's confession: everyone in the boat is stained by this, and the narrator too, because he is in the boat.

The last line is the one I keep returning to. "Both pipes smoked out" — Stubb's pipe and the whale's spout — and then Stubb standing "thoughtfully eyeing the vast corpse he had made." I don't know whether that thoughtfulness is remorse or only the satisfaction of a craftsman. I suspect Melville doesn't know either, and leaves the ashes on the water to say so.

annotations.quote: The waves, too, nodded their indolent crests; and across the wide trance of the sea, east nodded to west, and the sun over all.
annotations.note: The nodding spreads outward from three sleepy sailors until the compass points themselves are dozing. Melville lets syntax do the drowsing: short clauses, each a little dip of the head. It is the calm before the most violent chapter so far, and it is also, I think, the state Ishmael warned against back at [[ch35:Descartian vortices|the mast-head]] — the reverie that lets your foot slip.

annotations.quote: the whale looked like a portly burgher smoking his pipe of a warm afternoon. But that pipe, poor whale, was thy last.
annotations.note: A comic simile with a knife hidden in it. The whale is made cozy and human for exactly one sentence so that its death can land as a small murder. Notice Stubb is about to light his own pipe; the two smokers will be paired again in the final line.

annotations.quote: Start her, now; give ’em the long and strong stroke, Tashtego. Start her, Tash, my boy—start her, all; but keep cool, keep cool—cucumbers is the word
annotations.note: Stubb's whole philosophy in one breath: urgency and nonchalance at once, "grim death and grinning devils" and cucumbers. He is the book's great example of a man who survives horror by refusing to take it seriously. Whether that is wisdom or evasion is a question the book never quite closes.

annotations.quote: It was like holding an enemy’s sharp two-edged sword by the blade, and that enemy all the time striving to wrest it out of your clutch.
annotations.note: The Line chapter warned us abstractly; here the warning becomes skin. What strikes me is that the line is neither on the whale's side nor the men's — it is a third party, "magical," hot, alive, and it burns whoever touches it.

annotations.quote: you would have thought the craft had two keels—one cleaving the water, the other the air
annotations.note: A boat with a keel of taut rope pointing into the sky. Melville often reaches for these doubled images — ship and whale as two yoked bullocks, two heads on two sides — as if the world only made sense to him in pairs.

annotations.quote: The slanting sun playing upon this crimson pond in the sea, sent back its reflection into every face, so that they all glowed to each other like red men.
annotations.note: Tashtego is literally a "red man"; now the whole crew is. The blood erases the distinctions the ship otherwise keeps so carefully. It's one of the few places where Ishmael includes himself in the guilt without saying so.

annotations.quote: as if cautiously seeking to feel after some gold watch that the whale might have swallowed, and which he was fearful of breaking ere he could hook it out. But that gold watch he sought was the innermost life of the fish.
annotations.note: The most disturbing image in the chapter precisely because it is so gentle and so domestic. A man feeling delicately for a watch is a man being careful; here the care is aimed at finding a heart to burst. Melville loves to reveal cruelty through tenderness.

annotations.quote: “Yes; both pipes smoked out!” and withdrawing his own from his mouth, Stubb scattered the dead ashes over the water; and, for a moment, stood thoughtfully eyeing the vast corpse he had made.
annotations.note: Ashes scattered over water is a funeral gesture, and Stubb performs it without meaning to. "The vast corpse he had made" — not killed, made — treats the dead whale as a work. I read the pause as the closest Stubb ever comes to conscience.

links.why: The nodding trance that opens the kill is the mast-head reverie Ishmael warned about — the one where your foot slips.

links.q: All men live enveloped in whale-lines
links.why: The line blistering through Stubb's hands is The Line's abstract warning made into skin.
Stubb's 'thoughtful' pause over the corpse lasts about as long as it takes him to order a steak from it.
The very next chapter argues the harpooneer who did the hardest work here has been organized out of the credit.

ch62.essay:
A short chapter, and a strange one to find in a novel: it is an op-ed. Ishmael, who was in the boat pulling an oar a page ago, stops the story to argue that the whole fishery has organized its labor wrongly. The harpooneer rows himself to exhaustion, bawls himself hoarse, and then, at the one instant where everything depends on him, is asked to stand and throw with "what little strength may remain." Out of fifty chances, five hits. Ships come home with four barrels after four years. And the cause, he insists, is not the whale's speed but the man's breath.

I find this quietly moving because it is so plainly a worker's complaint dressed as an engineering note. "For one, I cannot bawl very heartily and work very recklessly at one and the same time" is Ishmael being honest about his own limits, and then generalizing them into a reform. The final line, about darting "from out of idleness, and not from out of toil," is offered as fishery advice but reads as a small creed about art, or attention, or anything that requires a clean instant of force. You cannot do the decisive thing well if you have spent yourself on the preliminaries.

It also makes me reread Stubb's kill. The harpoon was Tashtego's, the honor and the lance were Stubb's; the man who did the hardest work is already receding. The book will not let that stand unremarked.

annotations.quote: For one, I cannot bawl very heartily and work very recklessly at one and the same time.
annotations.note: Ishmael admitting he isn't a natural at the job. It is a small, human aside inside an argument, and it tells me the reform he proposes is partly a wish that the work could be made to fit men like him.

annotations.quote: no wonder that some sperm whalemen are absent four years with four barrels
annotations.note: Four years, four barrels — the rhythm makes a joke of a ruin. Behind it is a real economy: a voyage that failed like this could mean a crew paid almost nothing after years away.

annotations.quote: it is the harpooneer that makes the voyage, and if you take the breath out of his body how can you expect to find it there when most wanted!
annotations.note: Breath as a resource you can spend and then not have — and note that Queequeg, Tashtego and Daggoo, the three harpooneers, are the ship's three non-white men. The essay never says this, but it is arguing that the fishery squanders exactly the men it depends on most.

annotations.quote: To insure the greatest efficiency in the dart, the harpooneers of this world must start to their feet from out of idleness, and not from out of toil.
annotations.note: "Of this world" quietly widens the sentence beyond whaling. I read it as Melville's own theory of the decisive act: you can't strike true from the bottom of exhaustion. Idleness here is not laziness but reserve.

links.why: The kill this essay is complaining about — Tashtego rowed and threw; Stubb got the lance and the last word.
Knights and Squires introduces the three harpooneers the fishery, by Ishmael's argument, squanders.
Stubb's pitchpoling is the dart done from idleness — exactly the calm strike this chapter asks for.

ch63.essay:
"Out of the trunk, the branches grow; out of them, the twigs. So, in productive subjects, grow the chapters." This is Melville explaining, with a shrug, why the book is the shape it is, and I love that he does it in a chapter about a notched stick. The crotch is a small piece of wood that holds two harpoons ready. Fine. But what the chapter is really about is the second iron: the harpoon that, once the first one is thrown and the whale runs, is already tied to the running line and must be flung overboard somewhere, anywhere, or it will take a man's leg off inside the boat.

This is the kind of detail I would never have thought to want and cannot now forget. The second harpoon becomes "a dangling, sharp-edged terror, skittishly curvetting about both boat and whale," and you cannot get it back until the whale is dead. Now imagine four boats on one whale and eight or ten of these loose blades whipping around in the water. Melville ends by telling us plainly that he is planting this so that a later scene will make sense. He is, and it does; when we get to the last three days, this chapter is the thing that lets you see what is happening to Ahab's lines.

What I take from it: the book's digressions are load-bearing. The twigs are not decoration; they are where the fruit will hang.

annotations.quote: Out of the trunk, the branches grow; out of them, the twigs. So, in productive subjects, grow the chapters.
annotations.note: The book's own defense of its structure, in one sentence, placed at the head of a chapter about a stick. It is both an apology and a boast: the digressions are organic, not padding.

annotations.quote: It is a doubling of the chances.
annotations.note: Five words that hold the whole logic of the fishery: redundancy against a creature that can shake out one barb. And the next sentences show the cost of redundancy — the spare iron becomes the danger.

annotations.quote: it thenceforth becomes a dangling, sharp-edged terror, skittishly curvetting about both boat and whale
annotations.note: "Skittishly curvetting" is a horse's motion, playful and unpredictable, given to a blade. Melville makes the loose harpoon almost animate, a third creature in the fight that belongs to neither side.

annotations.quote: All these particulars are faithfully narrated here, as they will not fail to elucidate several most important, however intricate passages, in scenes hereafter to be painted.
annotations.note: A rare moment where the narrator shows his hand as a planner. Remember the loose second irons when Ahab's line fouls in [[ch135:the flag of Ahab|the final chase]]; this quiet chapter is what makes that catastrophe physically legible.

links.why: The loose second iron is planted here so that what happens to Ahab's line on the third day is physically legible.

links.q: All men live enveloped in whale-lines
links.why: The Line is the companion piece: the rope's danger, as this is the spare iron's.

links.q: God keep me from ever completing
links.why: 'Out of the trunk, the branches' is the same defense of digression Cetology makes at book length.

ch64.essay:
I find this chapter hard, and I have come to think I am meant to. It is a comedy built on a very old and very ugly stage joke — the white officer badgering the old Black cook, who is written in a dialect Melville lays on with a trowel — and for two or three pages it plays exactly as that joke would have played in a New York theater in 1850. And yet everything true in the chapter is said by Fleece, and the joke keeps turning until it lands on Stubb. "I'm bressed if he ain't more of shark dan Massa Shark hisself" is the last word, and Melville hands it to the cook and calls it "sage." So the question I keep asking is not whether the chapter is racist — parts of it plainly are, in the way the whole culture it came out of was — but what Melville is doing with the material. My answer, which I hold with some confidence, is that he is staging the joke in order to have it condemn the man telling it.

Look at the architecture. The chapter is three meals of the same animal, stacked. On deck, one man eats a steak by the light of a lamp burning the same whale's oil — Ishmael will spend the whole next chapter, [[ch65|The Whale as a Dish]], worrying at that oddity. Below the waterline, thousands of sharks eat the carcass in the dark, with a sound like "the smacking of their lips" that keeps the crew awake. And in the middle, the long paragraph on sharks: sea-fights, and then slave ships, where the sharks trot alongside "in case a parcel is to be carried anywhere." That word *parcel* is the darkest thing in the chapter and it is placed, I think deliberately, one page before the scene of a white officer bullying a Black man born in transit on a ferry crossing the Roanoke. Melville does not draw the line. He puts the two things next to each other and lets the reader draw it or fail to.

Then the sermon. Fleece is roused at midnight to preach to the sharks because Stubb wants a joke, and what comes out is better theology than anything Father Mapple said in New Bedford. "All angel is not'ing more dan de shark well goberned" — there is no third nature, no clean creature, only appetite and the governing of it. Compare Mapple's two-stranded lesson in [[ch9:Delight is to him|The Sermon]], which is about obedience and the delight of standing forth; Fleece's is about digestion. And Fleece knows his audience cannot hear him. The hungry can't listen and the full "sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral, and can't hear not'ing at all." That is a whole theory of why preaching fails, delivered by a ninety-year-old man in his nightshirt to a churning of fins, and Stubb, chewing, says he's "about of the same opinion." The benediction is a curse: fill your bellies till they burst, and then die. I read it as the truest blessing in the book because it wishes the sharks exactly what they will get — and it applies without alteration to the men above, and to the one pacing in the cabin.

Two smaller things. First, Ahab appears for a single paragraph, looks at the dead whale — the sight only "reminded him that Moby Dick was yet to be slain" — and goes below. The first kill of the voyage is, to its captain, a subtraction of time; the whole comic banquet happens in the space his indifference leaves open, and you can feel the ship relax when he goes. Second, the moment where the comedy stops: Fleece says that when he dies he "won't go nowhere; but some bressed angel will come and fetch him," and Melville writes that he says it "slowly, changing his whole air and demeanor." For one sentence the chapter takes him completely seriously. Then Stubb has to turn the tongs into a joke about the main-top, and I notice the joke has to work very hard to recover. That effort is the tell.

What I take from the chapter, finally, is a rule for reading the rest of the book: watch who gets the last word. Melville's officers talk more; his outsiders — Fleece here, Queequeg in [[ch66|The Shark Massacre]] with his "one dam Ingin," Pip later — talk less and are righter. The next time Stubb is charming, and he is charming often, I try to remember him eating by the whale's light and telling a man three times his age to be civil to sharks.

annotations.quote: as if the sight of that dead body reminded him that Moby Dick was yet to be slain; and though a thousand other whales were brought to his ship, all that would not one jot advance his grand, monomaniac object.
annotations.note: The first kill of the voyage is, for its captain, a disappointment. This line quietly tells you the ship's real economy: oil is for the owners; for Ahab every whale that isn't the White Whale is a subtraction of time.

annotations.quote: Stubb was a high liver; he was somewhat intemperately fond of the whale as a flavorish thing to his palate.
annotations.note: "Intemperately" is a loaded word aboard a ship whose owner's sister brought temperance ginger instead of grog — see the ginger scene in [[ch72:Ginger-jub|The Monkey-Rope]]. Stubb's appetite is presented as a small vice, and the whole chapter is about appetite: his, the sharks', and by the end of [[ch65]] yours.

annotations.quote: ship and whale, seemed yoked together like colossal bullocks, whereof one reclines while the other remains standing.
annotations.note: Two beasts in one yoke, one dead. It is a farm image, domestic and heavy, and it makes the ship a kind of animal too. Melville keeps refusing to let the Pequod be merely a machine.

annotations.quote: If you have never seen that sight, then suspend your decision about the propriety of devil-worship, and the expediency of conciliating the devil.
annotations.note: The long shark paragraph — sea-fights, slave ships — ends by proposing that the universe might reasonably be appeased rather than worshipped. It's a joke, but it is also Ahab's position stated by Ishmael, and the chapter goes on to stage exactly such a conciliation: Fleece preaching to the sharks.

annotations.quote: sharks also are the invariable outriders of all slave ships crossing the Atlantic, systematically trotting alongside, to be handy in case a parcel is to be carried anywhere, or a dead slave to be decently buried
annotations.note: "A parcel." The euphemism is doing terrible work, and Melville knows it. Dropped in the middle of a comic chapter about a steak, this is the book's darkest sentence about America, and it precedes by a page the scene of a white officer bullying a Black cook who was born on a ferry crossing the Roanoke.

annotations.quote: You is sharks, sartin; but if you gobern de shark in you, why den you be angel; for all angel is not’ing more dan de shark well goberned.
annotations.note: The most serious moral sentence in the chapter, put in the mouth of the character the chapter is laughing at. An angel is only a governed appetite; there is no third nature. I think Melville believed this, and I think that is why the sermon is given to Fleece rather than to Mapple.

annotations.quote: for den dey sink in de sea, go fast to sleep on de coral, and can’t hear not’ing at all, no more, for eber and eber.
annotations.note: Fleece's account of why preaching fails: the hungry can't listen, and the full fall asleep forever. It is a small, bleak parable about the uselessness of sermons to the living, and Stubb, eating, says he's "about of the same opinion."

annotations.quote: “Cussed fellow-critters! Kick up de damndest row as ever you can; fill your dam’ bellies ’till dey bust—and den die.”
annotations.note: The benediction is a curse. I read it as the truest blessing in the book: it wishes the sharks exactly what they will get. Note that it applies as well to the men on deck, and to the one at the capstan.

annotations.quote: “’Hind de hatchway, in ferry-boat, goin’ ober de Roanoke.”
annotations.note: Born on a ferry, in transit, belonging to no shore — a biography of one line. Stubb wants a "country"; Fleece was born between two. Melville gives the old man a birth that is both a joke and a whole history of displacement.

annotations.quote: “When dis old brack man dies,” said the negro slowly, changing his whole air and demeanor, “he hisself won’t go nowhere; but some bressed angel will come and fetch him.”
annotations.note: The one moment where the comedy stops. Fleece's tone changes, and for a sentence the chapter takes him completely seriously — before Stubb turns his pointing tongs into a joke about the main-top. I notice the joke has to work hard to recover.

annotations.quote: Don’t I always say that to be good, a whale-steak must be tough? There are those sharks now over the side, don’t you see they prefer it tough and rare?
annotations.note: Stubb aligns his own taste with the sharks' as a joke, and the joke is the thesis: he wants what they want, rarer. Fleece will make the alignment explicit in the last line. Notice how much of the chapter's meaning Stubb says himself without hearing it.

annotations.quote: Now, look here, bred’ren, just try wonst to be cibil, a helping yourselbs from dat whale. Don’t be tearin’ de blubber out your neighbour’s mout, I say.
annotations.note: The sermon's practical ethic: not abstinence, just don't take from your neighbour's mouth. It is the most modest moral proposal in the book and the sharks ignore it entirely. Ishmael's own version of this ethic comes in [[ch94:squeeze ourselves into each other|A Squeeze of the Hand]] — and he is just as unsure it can be kept.

annotations.quote: “Wish, by gor! whale eat him, ’stead of him eat whale. I’m bressed if he ain’t more of shark dan Massa Shark hisself,” muttered the old man
annotations.note: Fleece gets the last word, and it is the chapter's verdict: the one who preached civility to the sharks was the shark. Melville calls it a "sage ejaculation" without irony.

links.why: Ishmael takes the oddity of this supper — eating the whale by the whale's light — and turns it on the reader: who is not a cannibal?
Father Mapple's sermon is the official theology; put it beside Fleece's and decide which one the book actually believes.
The next night, the sharks from this chapter are massacred, and Queequeg gets a last word as blunt as Fleece's.
The whale being eaten here is the one Stubb killed a few pages ago; his pause over the corpse is the closest he comes to conscience.
Stubb the bully of the cook is also Stubb who gets Queequeg his grog — he is never only one thing.

ch65.essay:
The chapter begins with a puzzle Melville finds "outlandish": a man eating a creature by the light of its own oil. Then it wanders — French whale tongues, Henry VIII's porpoise sauce, Dutch "fritters" that look like doughnuts, ship-biscuit fried in the try-pots — and only in the last two paragraphs does it turn and bite. "Cannibals? who is not a cannibal?" The Fijian who salted a missionary against famine will fare better at judgment, we're told, than the diner who nails geese to the ground for their livers.

What I like is the way the argument uses the reader's own hands. Your knife handle is the bone of the ox's brother. You pick your teeth with a feather of the goose you ate. The secretary of the Society for the Suppression of Cruelty to Ganders signs his circulars with a goose quill. Stubb's crime, eating the whale by the whale's light, turns out to be everyone's ordinary condition; we all consume the animal and then use the rest of it to pretend we didn't.

I am also fond of the calves'-brains joke — young bucks eating brains until they grow enough of their own to tell a calf's head from their own — because it sneaks the book's anxiety about knowledge into a dinner. Does eating the whale, describing the whale, anatomizing the whale, ever give us the whale's mind? The chapter's honest answer is that it gives us supper.

annotations.quote: That mortal man should feed upon the creature that feeds his lamp, and, like Stubb, eat him by his own light, as you may say
annotations.note: The whole chapter hangs on this small, real oddity. It's the kind of thing only someone who had actually stood at a capstan by a sperm-oil lantern would think to be troubled by.

annotations.quote: when you come to sit down before a meat-pie nearly one hundred feet long, it takes away your appetite.
annotations.note: A joke about scale that is also the book's recurring problem: the whale is too big to be a dish, a subject, a chapter, or a symbol. Everything that tries to contain it fails in the same way.

annotations.quote: In the long try watches of the night it is a common thing for the seamen to dip their ship-biscuit into the huge oil-pots and let them fry there awhile. Many a good supper have I thus made.
annotations.note: Ishmael, who is often so lofty, is here a hungry sailor frying biscuit in whale fat at midnight. I trust the book more for lines like this; they are the ballast under the metaphysics.

annotations.quote: The head looks a sort of reproachfully at him, with an “Et tu Brute!” expression.
annotations.note: The calf's head betrayed by the diner who ate his brothers' brains. It's absurd, but it rehearses the book's real question about the whale's head hanging alongside: does the eaten thing have an expression, and can we read it?

annotations.quote: Cannibals? who is not a cannibal?
annotations.note: The line the chapter has been circling. Queequeg was introduced as a cannibal for the reader to fear — [[ch3:sober cannibal|'better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian']] — and now the category is universal. Melville's method throughout is to take the word that marks the outsider and hand it back to the reader.

annotations.quote: civilized and enlightened gourmand, who nailest geese to the ground and feastest on their bloated livers in thy paté-de-foie-gras.
annotations.note: The Fijian famine cannibal comes off better than the Parisian diner, and Melville says so in the second person. The comedy of the chapter has been cover for a moral ambush, and the archaic "nailest... feastest" lends it a scriptural sound.

annotations.quote: And with what quill did the Secretary of the Society for the Suppression of Cruelty to Ganders formally indite his circulars?
annotations.note: The last turn of the screw. Even the reformer writes his protest with the victim's feather; the society has, as of last month, switched to steel pens. Hypocrisy here isn't a scandal, just the ordinary texture of using things.

links.why: The supper this chapter is a footnote to — and Fleece's sermon on the shark in every one of us.
'Better sleep with a sober cannibal than a drunken Christian' — the word cannibal was handed to the reader first as a scare.
Queequeg's head as a cannibal George Washington: the book's first joke about who the cannibals really are.

ch66.essay:
Four paragraphs, and one of the most nightmarish images in the book. The night after Stubb's supper, Queequeg and another sailor hang lanterns over the side and spend the anchor-watch spading sharks in the skull. Melville had already said the sea looked like one huge cheese and the sharks the maggots in it; now he watches the maggots eat each other, and then eat themselves — a wounded shark bending "like flexible bows" to bite its own entrails, so that the same guts are "swallowed over and over again by the same mouth, to be oppositely voided by the gaping wound."

The phrase I keep hold of is "a sort of generic or Pantheistic vitality" that lurks in the joints after "the individual life had departed." A dead shark hauled on deck nearly takes Queequeg's hand off. This is horror, but it's also a thought Melville returns to constantly: that life might not be personal at all, that what animates a body is a general force that outlives the individual and does not care about him. It's the same idea that makes the whale's dead head able to "speak" to Ahab a few chapters on, and the same idea that frightens Ishmael in the whiteness of the whale.

Queequeg's line at the end is the human answer. Whatever god made the shark, "Fejee god or Nantucket god," must be "one dam Ingin." He does not theologize; he curses. I find that more honest than most of what the book's white characters say about Providence.

annotations.quote: would have almost thought the whole round sea was one huge cheese, and those sharks the maggots in it.
annotations.note: The ocean as a cheese. It's grotesque and comic and, I think, the most contemptuous image of the sea in the book — not sublime, not deep, just food going bad.

annotations.quote: like flexible bows, bent round, and bit their own; till those entrails seemed swallowed over and over again by the same mouth, to be oppositely voided by the gaping wound.
annotations.note: A closed loop of appetite: eating yourself through your own wound. It's the image Fleece's sermon was really about — appetite with no possible satisfaction — made literal.

annotations.quote: A sort of generic or Pantheistic vitality seemed to lurk in their very joints and bones, after what might be called the individual life had departed.
annotations.note: One of the book's central fears stated as a natural observation. If life is generic and not individual, then a person is only a temporary knot in it. The dead shark that bites is a small proof — and it is the same idea that makes Ahab expect a dead head to speak in [[ch70]], and that hollows out the color white in [[ch42:elusive something in the innermost|The Whiteness of the Whale]].

annotations.quote: “Queequeg no care what god made him shark,” said the savage, agonizingly lifting his hand up and down; “wedder Fejee god or Nantucket god; but de god wat made shark must be one dam Ingin.”
annotations.note: The chapter's only line of speech, and its conclusion. Queequeg treats all gods as equally answerable for the shark. "Ingin" is a slur turned back on the maker of things, by a man the crew calls a savage.

links.why: The sharks Fleece preached to are the ones being spaded here; appetite eating itself is his sermon made literal.

links.q: Speak, thou vast and venerable head
links.why: 'Pantheistic vitality' in a dead shark is the same fear that makes Ahab think a dead head might answer.
Life as generic rather than personal is the horror underneath the whiteness chapter.

ch67.essay:
Melville turns a butcher's job into a liturgy. It is Sunday, a Sabbath, and the whalemen are "ex officio professors of Sabbath breaking"; the ship becomes a shamble and every sailor a butcher, "offering up ten thousand red oxen to the sea gods." Then the long second paragraph does something I find astonishing: it makes you feel the ship's body. The blubber hook bites, the crew heaves, and the Pequod "careens over on her side; every bolt in her starts like the nail-heads of an old house in frosty weather; she trembles, quivers, and nods her frighted mast-heads to the sky." The ship suffers to peel the whale.

The technical image at the center — the blubber comes off in a spiral, like the peel of an orange, and the whale rolls over and over in the water as it's stripped — is so exact that it's beautiful. And the strip, dripping blood, rises to the main-top and hangs there "as if let down from the sky," a piece of the animal ascending. I'm not sure Melville intends a parody of resurrection, but the Sabbath opening makes it hard not to see one.

The last sentence is a small masterpiece of syntax: eight things happening at once, joined by commas, ending with "all hands swearing occasionally, by way of assuaging the general friction." That is the ship as a single working organism, and the swearing is its lubricant. I think this is the chapter where the Pequod stops being a setting and becomes a character.

annotations.quote: Ex officio professors of Sabbath breaking are all whalemen.
annotations.note: A joke that names the book's whole quarrel with land religion. Whalemen break the Sabbath by profession, and the chapter goes on to describe their work as a sacrifice — as if they had their own rite, older than the one they're breaking.

annotations.quote: every bolt in her starts like the nail-heads of an old house in frosty weather; she trembles, quivers, and nods her frighted mast-heads to the sky.
annotations.note: The ship is given nerves. That homely comparison — nails popping in a cold house — is exactly how Melville makes the sea familiar: by reaching for a New England winter.

annotations.quote: Now as the blubber envelopes the whale precisely as the rind does an orange, so is it stripped off from the body precisely as an orange is sometimes stripped by spiralizing it.
annotations.note: The single clearest technical image in the book. Once you have it, you can see the whole operation: the whale rolling like a spit as its coat unwinds. Melville is a superb explainer when he wants to be.

annotations.quote: the prodigious blood-dripping mass sways to and fro as if let down from the sky
annotations.note: The strip of blubber, hauled to the masthead, looks as though it descended from heaven. On a Sabbath. I can't tell whether this is blasphemy or reverence; I suspect Melville would say those are the same motion seen from two sides.

annotations.quote: the blubber-room gentlemen coiling, the mates scarfing, the ship straining, and all hands swearing occasionally, by way of assuaging the general friction.
annotations.note: The whole ship as one machine, and swearing as its oil. It's a sentence you can hear working, and it's the most affectionate portrait of collective labor in the book.

links.why: The strip of blubber peeled here is what the next chapter argues is the whale's skin.
Mapple's pulpit and this Sabbath of butchery are the book's two rites; the whalemen have their own, older one.

links.q: Look not too long in the face of the fire
links.why: The Try-Works is the next stage of this industrial liturgy, and the one where it becomes hell.

ch68.essay:
This chapter begins as a pedant's quarrel — what, exactly, is the whale's skin? — and ends as a sermon addressed, as far as I can tell, to me. I want to explain why a chapter about blubber is one of the four or five in the book I would not give up.

The argument itself is simple. The blubber, Ishmael says, is the skin; the infinitely thin isinglass film you can scrape off a dead whale with your hand is only "the skin of the skin." What matters is how he holds the opinion: "My original opinion remains unchanged; but it is only an opinion." That sentence is the fine print under all of the book's confident cetology, and I trust the confident parts more because it is there. Then comes the detail I keep returning to. He keeps dried scraps of that transparent film as bookmarks in his whale-books, and fancies that reading through them magnifies the page: "it is pleasant to read about whales through their own spectacles." That is the entire method of Moby-Dick stated as a joke — look at the whale through the whale — together with the admission that the magnification is imagined. Every chapter from [[ch32|Cetology]] onward is a page read through a scrap of skin.

The second movement is about writing. The whale's flanks are cross-hatched like an Italian engraving, and over the hatching are other marks, "hieroglyphical," like the ones on the Indian rocks up the Mississippi, and "the mystic-marked whale remains undecipherable." Two chapters from now, in [[ch70:Speak, thou vast and venerable head|The Sphynx]], Ahab will lean over a severed head and demand that it speak; here, a chapter earlier and in a naturalist's flat voice, the book has already said the writing on the whale has no known key. And much later, in [[ch79:I but put that brow before you|The Prairie]], Ishmael will put the whale's brow in front of you and say "read it if you can." The Blanket is where that refusal is first stated, and it is stated about skin, which is the only part of the whale we ever actually touch. (I would add that Queequeg is also covered in writing no one can read — his tattoos, in [[ch110:Queequeg in his coffin|Queequeg in His Coffin]], are "a complete theory of the heavens and the earth" that even he cannot decipher. The book's two undecipherable bodies are the whale's and the harpooneer's.)

And then the turn that makes the chapter. The whale is warm-blooded. It lives to its lips in Arctic water and is warmer inside than a man in Borneo — Melville's actual comparison is uglier than that and I have left it in the notes. From the fact of a thick coat and a warm interior, he draws advice: "Oh, man! admire and model thyself after the whale! Do thou, too, remain warm among ice. Do thou, too, live in this world without being of it." The second sentence is scriptural — in the world but not of it — but the model is not a saint; it is an animal with thick walls. I find this consoling and strange, and I think it is the book's real counsel for surviving Ahab's ship. Starbuck cannot do it; his temperature is set by the captain's. Stubb does it by not caring, which is a different thing. Ishmael does it by exactly this: keeping a private warmth, a curiosity, that the voyage cannot chill. When he is the only one left floating at the end, it is, in a sense, because of the blanket.

Then the last line takes it back a little — "how easy and how hopeless to teach these fine things! Of erections, how few are domed like St. Peter's!" — and this double motion, exhort and then admit the exhortation is useless, is the most Melville thing in the chapter. He gives you the rule and the reason you can't follow it, in the same breath, and leaves you to keep what warmth you can.

annotations.quote: My original opinion remains unchanged; but it is only an opinion.
annotations.note: Ishmael being scrupulous about the limits of what he knows. The book is full of confident cetology, and lines like this are the fine print. I like him better for it.

annotations.quote: At any rate, it is pleasant to read about whales through their own spectacles, as you may say.
annotations.note: He reads his whale-books through a dried scrap of whale skin and pretends it magnifies. This is the book's method confessed: to look at the whale through the whale, and to know the magnification is imagined.

annotations.quote: is not so much to be regarded as the skin of the creature, as the skin of the skin, so to speak
annotations.note: A phrase that sounds like a joke and isn't quite. The whale has layers on layers, and each one you strip reveals another surface, not a depth. This is the whole problem of knowing the whale in miniature.

annotations.quote: something like those in the finest Italian line engravings. But these marks do not seem to be impressed upon the isinglass substance above mentioned, but seem to be seen through it
annotations.note: The marks are under the transparent film, not on it — writing seen through a window. It's a precise observation and also a picture of the reader's situation: we see the whale's meaning through a layer we can't remove. The same word, engraving, will describe Queequeg's tattooed body.

annotations.quote: Like those mystic rocks, too, the mystic-marked whale remains undecipherable.
annotations.note: The whale's flanks are hieroglyphics that cannot be read. Ahab will spend the next chapter demanding that a head "speak"; Ishmael has already told us, calmly, that the writing on the whale has no known key.

annotations.quote: the blood of a Polar whale is warmer than that of a Borneo negro in summer.
annotations.note: The fact that turns the chapter. A creature that must stay warm, living permanently in ice: Melville sees in it a moral possibility, not just a wonder.

annotations.quote: Oh, man! admire and model thyself after the whale! Do thou, too, remain warm among ice. Do thou, too, live in this world without being of it.
annotations.note: Advice from blubber. "In this world without being of it" is scriptural language, but the model here is not a saint; it is an animal with thick walls and a warm interior. I take it as the book's counsel for surviving Ahab's ship: keep your own temperature.

annotations.quote: But how easy and how hopeless to teach these fine things! Of erections, how few are domed like St. Peter’s! of creatures, how few vast as the whale!
annotations.note: The sermon undercuts itself immediately. It's easy to say "be like the whale" and hopeless to do it, because the whale's virtue is its size. This double motion — exhort, then admit the exhortation is useless — is very Melville.

links.q: Speak, thou vast and venerable head
links.why: Two chapters on, Ahab demands that a whale's head speak; this chapter has already said, calmly, that the whale is undecipherable.

links.q: I but put that brow before you
links.why: The Prairie is the full-dress version of 'read it if you can' — the whale's brow as an unreadable face.
Queequeg's tattoos are the book's other body covered in writing no one can read.

links.q: God keep me from ever completing
links.why: Cetology is where the whole project of knowing the whale is declared unfinishable; The Blanket is that project down at the level of skin.
Bulkington's 'landlessness' and the whale's 'warm among ice' are the book's two pictures of how to live unsheltered.

ch69.essay:
The stripped whale, headless and white as marble, is cut loose and drifts away under a mild blue sky, swarmed by sharks and screaming birds, "till lost in infinite perspectives." Melville calls it a funeral and then makes the mourners the eaters: "the sea-vultures all in pious mourning, the air-sharks all punctiliously in black or speckled." It's savage about ceremony. The birds are dressed for the occasion because they are dressed to eat.

But the part that stays with me is the second movement, where the corpse becomes a ghost. Some timid navy ship sees the white mass from far off, mistakes it for breakers, and writes in the log "shoals, rocks, and breakers hereabouts: beware!" — and for years ships avoid a spot where nothing ever was. "There's your law of precedents; there's your utility of traditions... There's orthodoxy!" A dead animal becomes a superstition becomes a chart. The book has been asking what the White Whale is, and here is one answer: a white shape that made someone afraid once and got written down.

The last line — "Are you a believer in ghosts, my friend?" — is addressed to me, and I find I don't have a clean answer. Not the Cock-Lane kind. But the kind that gets into logbooks, yes, I believe in those.

annotations.quote: The peeled white body of the beheaded whale flashes like a marble sepulchre
annotations.note: The whale, stripped, has become white — the color the book is most afraid of. What was dark and alive is now pale and monumental; this is a small preview of the White Whale as an image of death.

annotations.quote: Beneath the unclouded and mild azure sky, upon the fair face of the pleasant sea, wafted by the joyous breezes, that great mass of death floats on and on, till lost in infinite perspectives.
annotations.note: Every adjective in the setting is gentle — mild, fair, pleasant, joyous — and the object in it is a mass of death. Melville's indifferent universe in one sentence: nature doesn't dim for a funeral.

annotations.quote: The sea-vultures all in pious mourning, the air-sharks all punctiliously in black or speckled.
annotations.note: The birds are sharks and the sharks are vultures and both are mourners dressed for the funeral of the thing they're eating. It's an attack on every pious crowd at every grave, and Melville does it with the word "punctiliously."

annotations.quote: Oh, horrible vultureism of earth! from which not the mightiest whale is free.
annotations.note: The sentence widens from this one corpse to the earth as a whole, and the point is that size is no protection. Ahab thinks the White Whale is exempt from the ordinary fate; this chapter says nothing is.

annotations.quote: leaping over it as silly sheep leap over a vacuum, because their leader originally leaped there when a stick was held.
annotations.note: The famous sheep image for tradition: the obstacle is gone and everyone still jumps. That the "obstacle" was a dead whale's corpse makes the fable stranger — the thing being avoided was never dangerous, only large and white.

annotations.quote: There’s your law of precedents; there’s your utility of traditions; there’s the story of your obstinate survival of old beliefs never bottomed on the earth, and now not even hovering in the air! There’s orthodoxy!
annotations.note: From a whale carcass to a charge against all inherited belief in four clauses. I hear real anger here, and I think it is directed at church and law alike. The corpse's "ghost" is any rule whose reason has been eaten away.

annotations.quote: Are you a believer in ghosts, my friend? There are other ghosts than the Cock-Lane one, and far deeper men than Doctor Johnson who believe in them.
annotations.note: The chapter ends by turning to the reader. The Cock-Lane ghost was an 18th-century hoax Johnson investigated; Melville is saying the real ghosts are the ones in charts and creeds, and that serious people do believe in those.

links.why: A white mass that frightened someone once and got written down — this is one answer to what the White Whale is.
Ahab's Moby Dick is built exactly like this ghost: rumor, dread, and a chart entry.
The mourners dressed to eat are the sharks Fleece preached to.

ch70.essay:
Noon; a copper calm "like a universal yellow lotus"; the crew below at dinner; and Ahab alone on deck with the severed head hanging at the ship's side. He takes Stubb's spade for a crutch, leans over, and talks to it. This is the chapter where I first understood what Ahab actually wants, and it isn't revenge. He wants the head to tell him what it saw down there — the drowned lovers, the murdered mate, "unrecorded names and navies" rusting where the whale slept. "O head! thou hast seen enough to split the planets and make an infidel of Abraham, and not one syllable is thine!" The complaint is not that the world is cruel. It is that the world will not explain itself.

I want to be precise about why this is the philosophical center of the book and not just its most beautiful monologue. Go back to the quarter-deck, to [[ch36:pasteboard masks|the speech about the pasteboard mask]]: all visible objects are masks, and Ahab means to strike through the mask to whatever is behind it. The Sphynx is what happens when he gets a piece of the mask in his hands. He has killed a whale, cut off its head, hung it from the ship — and it is still a mask. It will not speak. So the chapter is the first experimental result of Ahab's whole program, and the result is silence. Ishmael has already told us in [[ch68:the mystic-marked whale remains undecipherable|The Blanket]] that the whale's writing has no key; Ahab, who did not read that chapter, finds out the hard way. What he does with the silence is the disease: he treats it as withholding rather than absence. A head that has "seen enough" and says nothing is, to Ahab, a witness refusing to testify. To Ishmael, it is a head.

The staging is exact. The head is "black and hooded," and hangs from the ship's waist "like the giant Holofernes's from the girdle of Judith" — so the Pequod is Judith, the whale a beheaded tyrant, and Ahab is interrogating his own trophy. He props his wounded body on the spade that helped do the beheading. And notice how much tenderness there is in the speech. The "locked lovers" leaping from a burning ship, "true to each other, when heaven seemed false to them" — this is not the voice of a monster. It is the voice of someone who believes fidelity is possible between people and impossible from the sky, and who has organized his life around the second half of that belief. In [[ch132:wife and child|The Symphony]], almost at the end, you will hear the same tenderness turned toward his own wife and child, and it will fail to save him for the same reason it fails here: he cannot stop asking the sky.

Then "Sail ho!" and the mood flips entirely — "that's cheering," "Would now St. Paul would come along that way" — and in the flush of it he says the line I would choose if I had to choose one for the whole novel: "not the smallest atom stirs or lives on matter, but has its cunning duplicate in mind." Everything outside corresponds to something inside. That is Ahab's faith and it is also his disease, because if the world is a mirror, then the whale that took his leg means something and can be made to answer. It is also, I should say, very nearly Melville's own faith — the book is built on "linked analogies," on the try-works being hell and the monkey-rope being marriage — which is why the novel can never simply refute Ahab. It shares his premise and fears his conclusion. You can watch Ishmael test the same idea and pull back from it in [[ch99:some certain significance lurks|The Doubloon]], where everyone reads the coin and each reading is a self-portrait.

One more thing, easy to miss. "That lively cry upon this deadly calm might almost convert a better man." Ahab knows what he is. The line is light, thrown off, and it is the closest he ever comes to admitting he could have been otherwise. The lotus keeps unfolding its "noiseless measureless leaves"; the head hangs; the breeze comes. Nothing has been answered and the ship sails on.

annotations.quote: there, that blood-dripping head hung to the Pequod’s waist like the giant Holofernes’s from the girdle of Judith.
annotations.note: Judith beheaded the tyrant to save her city; here the ship wears the trophy. The comparison flatters the kill and quietly asks whether this beheading saved anyone. Also: Ahab is about to speak to the head Judith would have simply displayed.

annotations.quote: An intense copper calm, like a universal yellow lotus, was more and more unfolding its noiseless measureless leaves upon the sea.
annotations.note: One of the most beautiful sentences in the book, and it's about nothing happening. The lotus is a Buddhist emblem of contemplation; the calm opens like a flower so that Ahab can walk into it alone.

annotations.quote: placed its other end crutch-wise under one arm, and so stood leaning over with eyes attentively fixed on this head.
annotations.note: The spade that helped behead the whale becomes Ahab's crutch — he leans his wounded body on the instrument of the kill. The staging is exact: a crippled man propped up by violence, questioning its result.

annotations.quote: “Speak, thou vast and venerable head,” muttered Ahab, “which, though ungarnished with a beard, yet here and there lookest hoary with mosses; speak, mighty head, and tell us the secret thing that is in thee.
annotations.note: "The secret thing that is in thee" — Ahab wants the head as a witness, not a trophy. The whale has been to the bottom; Ahab hasn't. This is envy dressed as command.

annotations.quote: where in her murderous hold this frigate earth is ballasted with bones of millions of the drowned
annotations.note: The earth as a ship whose ballast is the dead. It's Ahab's cosmology in a clause: the world floats level only because of what it has killed.

annotations.quote: Thou saw’st the locked lovers when leaping from their flaming ship; heart to heart they sank beneath the exulting wave; true to each other, when heaven seemed false to them.
annotations.note: Ahab, who we think of as all rage, imagines drowning lovers with real tenderness. "True to each other, when heaven seemed false" is his own creed: fidelity among people is possible; fidelity from the sky is not.

annotations.quote: O head! thou hast seen enough to split the planets and make an infidel of Abraham, and not one syllable is thine!”
annotations.note: The head's silence is the injury. If the whale could speak, its testimony would break the faith of Abraham himself; that it cannot leaves Ahab with a witness who will not testify. This is the book's whole theology of the unanswering world.

annotations.quote: That lively cry upon this deadly calm might almost convert a better man.
annotations.note: A sail sighted, and Ahab jokes about his own damnation. "A better man" — he knows what he is. The line is light, and it is the closest he comes to admitting he could have been otherwise.

annotations.quote: “Aye? Well, now, that’s cheering,” cried Ahab, suddenly erecting himself, while whole thunder-clouds swept aside from his brow.
annotations.note: Watch how fast the weather changes on Ahab's face. He can be pulled out of the abyss by a sail, a breeze, a bit of news — which tells me the despair, though real, is also a posture he steps out of when the hunt calls. The same instant reversal happens when the Rachel hails in [[ch128:my boy, my own boy|The Pequod Meets the Rachel]], and there he steps the other way.

annotations.quote: O Nature, and O soul of man! how far beyond all utterance are your linked analogies! not the smallest atom stirs or lives on matter, but has its cunning duplicate in mind.”
annotations.note: If I had to pick one sentence as the key to Ahab, it's this. Every outer thing has an inner twin. That belief is what lets him read a whale as malice and a wind as a message; it's also what the book, through Ishmael, keeps testing and never quite denies.

links.why: The quarter-deck speech is the program; The Sphynx is its first experimental result, and the result is silence.
Ishmael has already said the whale cannot be read; Ahab finds it out by asking.

links.q: I but put that brow before you
links.why: The Prairie repeats this scene in Ishmael's key — the brow put before you to read, if you can.
The Doubloon is 'linked analogies' tested on a coin: every reader sees himself.
The tenderness Ahab shows the drowned lovers here comes back, aimed at his own family, in The Symphony.

ch71.essay:
The second of the Pequod's nine encounters with other ships, and the first that feels like a warning aimed straight at Ahab. The Jeroboam has plague aboard, a captain too scrupulous to come alongside, and a freckled little man in a walnut-colored coat who claims to be the archangel Gabriel and has taken over the ship by sheer force of conviction. Melville's account of how a fanatic captures a crew — "the measureless self-deception of the fanatic himself" mattering less than "his measureless power of deceiving and bedevilling so many others" — is, I think, deliberately placed next to Ahab. We just watched Ahab bind his crew with a gold coin and a ritual. Here is the same thing in a cracked mirror.

The story of Macey is told flatly and is horrifying for it: the mate lifted into the air by a white shadow, landing fifty yards off, "not a chip of the boat was harmed, nor a hair of any oarsman's head; but the mate for ever sank." Moby Dick does not destroy; he selects. And Gabriel, who prophesied doom in the general way any madman does, gets credit for having predicted it precisely.

The letter is the chapter's real cruelty. A wife's "pinny hand" addressed to a man who's been dead a year; Ahab reads the name aloud before he understands; Gabriel impales it on a knife and sends it back — "thou art soon going that way." The Pequod carries the mail for the dead. The book will not let us forget that everyone on the sea is someone's unanswered letter.

annotations.quote: yet conscientiously adhering to the timid quarantine of the land, he peremptorily refused to come into direct contact with the Pequod.
annotations.note: Captain Mayhew observes a land rule at sea, and Ishmael calls it timid. But note the effect: the whole conversation is shouted across water, boat lurching, and the Jeroboam becomes a ship you can hear but never board — exactly like the future.

annotations.quote: A deep, settled, fanatic delirium was in his eyes.
annotations.note: We're told about Gabriel's eyes before his name. Compare Ahab, whose eyes are also the first thing the crew reads. The book keeps a small catalogue of mad gazes, and this is its most explicit.

annotations.quote: announcing the speedy opening of the seventh vial, which he carried in his vest-pocket; but, which, instead of containing gunpowder, was supposed to be charged with laudanum.
annotations.note: The apocalypse in a waistcoat, and the vial of wrath is full of opium. Melville's contempt for Gabriel is comic and precise; he lets the prophet's props expose him.

annotations.quote: Nor is the history of fanatics half so striking in respect to the measureless self-deception of the fanatic himself, as his measureless power of deceiving and bedevilling so many others.
annotations.note: This sentence is about Gabriel and it is aimed at Ahab. The Pequod's crew was won over in [[ch36:little lower layer|The Quarter-Deck]] by the same means: unflinching earnestness and fear. The Jeroboam is the Pequod with the mask off.

annotations.quote: pronouncing the White Whale to be no less a being than the Shaker God incarnated
annotations.note: For Gabriel, Moby Dick is God. For Ahab, he is the mask over some malice. The two madmen disagree about the whale's identity and agree completely that it is more than an animal — which is the disease the book is diagnosing.

annotations.quote: Not a chip of the boat was harmed, nor a hair of any oarsman’s head; but the mate for ever sank.
annotations.note: The most chilling thing about the White Whale isn't force but selection. He takes one man and touches nothing else. Whether that reads as intelligence or accident is precisely the question Ahab cannot leave alone.

annotations.quote: instead of only making a general prophecy, which any one might have done, and so have chanced to hit one of many marks in the wide margin allowed.
annotations.note: Ishmael quietly explains how prophecy works: predict doom vaguely, wait, take credit. It's a rationalist's footnote in a chapter full of omens, and it applies to every prophet in the book, including Elijah on the Nantucket wharf.

annotations.quote: Of such a letter, Death himself might well have been the post-boy.
annotations.note: A letter kept so long in a dark locker that it has grown mould, addressed to a man already drowned. Whaling ships carried mail for years on the chance of meeting the right ship; most letters, Ishmael says, never arrive. The Pequod is a floating dead-letter office.

annotations.quote: “Nay, keep it thyself,” cried Gabriel to Ahab; “thou art soon going that way.”
annotations.note: The dead mate's letter is offered to Ahab as if he were the addressee. Gabriel's prophecies are vague and self-serving, but the book lets this one be accurate, and Ahab's response is not argument but a curse.

links.why: Ahab captured his crew on the quarter-deck by the same means Gabriel used — earnestness and fear. The Jeroboam is the Pequod with the mask off.
Elijah on the Nantucket wharf is the book's first vague prophet; Gabriel is its second, and Ishmael explains how their trick works.
Fedallah's prophecy is the one that is precise — compare Gabriel's general doom.
The book's last other-ship encounter: another letter of loss the Pequod refuses to carry.

ch72.essay:
This is the chapter I would hand to anyone who asked why the book's digressions matter, because it is a digression that turns, in the space of a paragraph, into the most generous thought in the novel. Here is the situation, which is real and was practiced on whaleships: Queequeg is down on the rolling, half-submerged whale in "a shirt and socks," among sharks, working a hundred-pound hook into the blubber. Ishmael stands on deck holding a rope tied to Queequeg's waist — and, by a custom peculiar to the Pequod, tied to his own. If Queequeg goes down, honor requires that Ishmael go with him. "We two, for the time, were wedded."

Then the thought. From a rope around two waists, Ishmael derives the whole condition of being a person: "my own individuality was now merged in a joint stock company of two"; his free will has "received a mortal wound"; and — this is the leap — this situation "was the precise situation of every mortal that breathes," except that most of us are tied not to one other person but to many. "If your banker breaks, you snap; if your apothecary by mistake sends you poison in your pills, you die." And then the line I think of more than almost any other in the book: "I only had the management of one end of it." You control your end, and only your end. The other end is someone else's care and someone else's luck.

I want to say why I find this so moving, and it is partly the placement. The book has been building a marriage between these two men since the Spouter-Inn — [[ch4:arm thrown over me|Queequeg's arm thrown over Ishmael in bed]], the pipe shared in [[ch10:no more my splintered heart|A Bosom Friend]], the wedding-joke language of "bosom friend" and "married." All of that was comedy, and the comedy was real. The monkey-rope keeps every bit of the affection and adds a death to it. The vow is now a contract with drowning in it. And notice the sad qualifier Ishmael can't help adding: "for the time." He is writing after the voyage; he knows which of them survived the other, and he knows that the thing which finally floats him out of the whirlpool in the [[epilogue|Epilogue]] is Queequeg's coffin — the last object the other man tied to him.

The second thing that moves me is how carefully Melville refuses to let it be solemn. A footnote tells you the tying-together was Stubb's invention, "an improvement upon the original usage," introduced to make the rope-holder pay attention — the sacred bond is also a management incentive. Then the scene collapses into the ginger business, Stubb roaring at Dough-Boy about Aunt Charity's temperance ginger-jub and getting Queequeg a real drink. So the chapter gives you both readings, the marriage and the mechanism, and declines to choose, which is exactly how the rest of the book handles every large idea: it says the thing, then shows you the deck it was said on. Compare [[ch60:All men live enveloped in whale-lines|The Line]], which reaches the same conclusion from the opposite side — the rope as the thing that can kill you, not the thing that holds you. Both chapters are true. Both are about a rope.

And the image I would put on the cover, if I had to pick one: Tashtego and Daggoo hacking at sharks inches from Queequeg's legs with their long spades, so that "those indiscreet spades of theirs would come nearer amputating a leg than a tail." Your friends, trying to kill your enemies, nearly kill you. Ishmael spells out the allegory himself, which he almost never does — "that unsounded ocean you gasp in, is Life; those sharks, your foes; those spades, your friends" — and then softens it with "poor lad." That is the book's picture of ordinary life: you are up to your neck, and help hurts, and someone on deck has the other end of the rope and is doing the best he can.

annotations.quote: It is much the same with him who endeavors the description of the scene. We must now retrace our way a little.
annotations.note: Ishmael admits the book can't be in two places at once, any more than a sailor can. The narrative's backtracking is presented as the same problem as the deck's chaos — a rare, honest glimpse of the writer at his own windlass.

annotations.quote: On the occasion in question, Queequeg figured in the Highland costume—a shirt and socks—in which to my eyes, at least, he appeared to uncommon advantage
annotations.note: Ishmael's frank pleasure in looking at Queequeg, dropped lightly into a technical account. The book's affection between these two men is never coy, and this is one of its warmest asides.

annotations.quote: So that for better or for worse, we two, for the time, were wedded
annotations.note: The marriage vow, literally. The bedroom scene in Nantucket was a joke about a marriage; the monkey-rope makes it a contract with death in it. "For the time" is the sad qualifier — Ishmael already knows one of them will survive the other.

annotations.quote: my own individuality was now merged in a joint stock company of two; that my free will had received a mortal wound
annotations.note: The American language of business — a joint stock company — used for the deepest kind of dependence. Ishmael loses his free will not to Ahab but to friendship, and finds he doesn't mind.

annotations.quote: I saw that this situation of mine was the precise situation of every mortal that breathes; only, in most cases, he, one way or other, has this Siamese connexion with a plurality of other mortals.
annotations.note: The rope generalized: every person is tied to many others whose errors can kill him. It's an unusually humane conclusion for this book, and it's reached by standing on a deck holding a friend over sharks.

annotations.quote: If your banker breaks, you snap; if your apothecary by mistake sends you poison in your pills, you die.
annotations.note: Ishmael's examples are deliberately landlocked and middle-class — a banker, a pharmacist — so that no reader can say the rope is only a whaleman's problem. It is the most direct address to the reader's own dependence in the book, and it comes from a man standing on a slippery deck holding a friend over sharks.

annotations.quote: Nor could I possibly forget that, do what I would, I only had the management of one end of it.*
annotations.note: The chapter's quiet thesis. You control your end and only your end; the other end is someone else's care and luck. I think of this line more than almost any other in the book.

annotations.quote: but it was only in the Pequod that the monkey and his holder were ever tied together. This improvement upon the original usage was introduced by no less a man than Stubb
annotations.note: The footnote deflates the metaphysics: the wedding was Stubb's idea, a management trick to keep the rope-holder honest. Melville lets you have both readings — the sacred bond and the incentive scheme — and doesn't choose.

annotations.quote: those indiscreet spades of theirs would come nearer amputating a leg than a tail.
annotations.note: Your friends, trying to kill your enemies, nearly kill you. It's funny and it's exact, and it gives the chapter its final parable: sharks and spades, foes and friends, both dangerous.

annotations.quote: That unsounded ocean you gasp in, is Life; those sharks, your foes; those spades, your friends; and what between sharks and spades you are in a sad pickle and peril, poor lad.
annotations.note: Ishmael spells out the allegory himself, which he rarely does, and then softens it with "poor lad." The whale-hunt as a picture of ordinary life: you are up to your neck, and help hurts.

annotations.quote: Ginger! is ginger the sort of fuel you use, Dough-boy, to kindle a fire in this shivering cannibal?
annotations.note: Stubb's outrage at temperance ginger-water is comedy, but it's also the ship's one act of care for Queequeg in the chapter. The man who bullied Fleece is the man who gets the harpooneer his grog. Stubb is never only one thing.

links.why: The first time the two men are bound together, in bed at the Spouter-Inn — a joke this chapter takes seriously.
A Bosom Friend is where the marriage was sealed; the monkey-rope is where it gets its terms.

links.q: All men live enveloped in whale-lines
links.why: The Line reaches the same conclusion from the other side: the rope that binds is the rope that kills.
What finally holds Ishmael up is the last thing Queequeg tied to him.
The other great chapter of Ishmael's fellow-feeling — hands in the spermaceti instead of a rope round the waist.

ch73.essay:
A second whale is killed almost as an afterthought — a Right Whale, which the crew disdains as "foul lard" — and the killing takes one paragraph of tremendous physical writing: the line scraping under the keel, the drops flying off it "like bits of broken glass," two boats towed in a full circle around the ship. Then the chapter becomes what its title promises: a talk.

Stubb and Flask, lashing flukes, discuss Fedallah. Stubb is sure he's the devil, tail coiled in his pocket, come to bargain for Ahab's soul in exchange for Moby Dick; Flask half-believes it and keeps asking the practical questions a child asks — how old is he, what if he ducks you back, what will you do with the tail. "Sell it for an ox whip when we get home;—what else?" It's the funniest exchange in the book and one of the most sinister, because everything Stubb says as a joke the plot will honor. Fedallah's bargain is real; the Parsee's shadow does lengthen Ahab's, in the chapter's last image, where Ahab stands so that the Parsee "occupied his shadow."

The reason for the second head, per Flask, is a charm from Fedallah: a ship with a Sperm Whale's head on one side and a Right Whale's on the other can never capsize. Ishmael's gloss — Locke's head on one side, Kant's on the other, and the ship sailing level "in very poor plight" — is his advice to throw all the philosophers overboard and float light. Ahab does not take it; he wants both heads. He wants the balance and the charm and the bargain. The mule carrying two panniers is the book's picture of a mind that has taken on too much.

annotations.quote: the drops fell like bits of broken glass on the water
annotations.note: Water flung off a taut line seen as glass — brittle, bright, sharp. Melville's physical eye at its best; you can see the sun on it. This one paragraph is the entire hunt, and it's over before the chapter's real subject arrives.

annotations.quote: did you never hear, Stubb, that that ship can never afterwards capsize?”
annotations.note: The whole point of the second whale is a sailors' charm passed on by Fedallah. Ahab, the great blasphemer, is hedging with superstition. The book lets us see that his rationalism was never the point.

annotations.quote: The reason why you don’t see his tail, is because he tucks it up out of sight; he carries it coiled away in his pocket, I guess.
annotations.note: Stubb's devil is a folk-tale devil with a hidden tail and oakum in his boots. It's absurd, and the absurdity is protective: a joke lets him say what the ship actually fears about the man who sleeps in the rigging.

annotations.quote: the old man is hard bent after that White Whale, and the devil there is trying to come round him, and get him to swap away his silver watch, or his soul, or something of that sort, and then he’ll surrender Moby Dick.”
annotations.note: The Faust plot, told as gossip by a second mate. "His silver watch, or his soul" — Stubb can't tell which is the higher price, and neither, I think, can Ahab. The joke is a prophecy, and the book keeps it.

annotations.quote: Doesn’t the devil live for ever; who ever heard that the devil was dead? Did you ever see any parson a wearing mourning for the devil?
annotations.note: Stubb's theology is more cheerful than Ahab's and just as bleak: evil is permanent and nobody mourns it. He says it while coiling a rope, which is how the book delivers most of its metaphysics.

annotations.quote: Who’s afraid of him, except the old governor who daresn’t catch him and put him in double-darbies, as he deserves, but lets him go about kidnapping people; aye, and signed a bond with him
annotations.note: "The old governor" is God, who in Stubb's fable has a deal with the devil to roast whoever the devil takes. It's Fleece's sermon again — a governor who won't govern — but from a white officer who thinks he's only joking.

annotations.quote: “Do with it? Sell it for an ox whip when we get home;—what else?”
annotations.note: Even the devil's tail is inventory. Stubb's genius is that nothing is too large or too dark to be priced, and it's why he sleeps well on a doomed ship.

annotations.quote: So, when on one side you hoist in Locke’s head, you go over that way; but now, on the other side, hoist in Kant’s and you come back again; but in very poor plight. Thus, some minds for ever keep trimming boat.
annotations.note: Empiricism on the starboard, idealism on the larboard, and the ship sails level only by carrying both dead weights. Ishmael's advice is to throw them overboard. Ahab keeps both heads, and the Pequod sails on "sorely strained."

annotations.quote: And Ahab chanced so to stand, that the Parsee occupied his shadow; while, if the Parsee’s shadow was there at all it seemed only to blend with, and lengthen Ahab’s.
annotations.note: After a chapter of jokes about the devil, one silent image confirms them: Fedallah stands inside Ahab's shadow and extends it. Whether he is a man or a familiar, the book lets the light say what the sailors only guess.

links.why: Stubb's joke about the devil's bargain is the Faust plot the book actually runs; here is the contract's small print.
The Parsee lengthening Ahab's shadow ends, on the second day, with Fedallah gone before him.
The two heads Ahab is balancing get their tour in the next two chapters.
Stubb's 'old governor' who won't govern is Fleece's sermon again, from the other side of the color line.

ch74.essay:
"Here, now, are two great whales, laying their heads together; let us join them, and lay together our own." The pun is the invitation, and the chapter is a walk around and then into a sperm whale's head. What it finds is the eye — tiny, lashless, "a young colt's eye" — set so far to each side that the whale can see neither straight ahead nor behind, and must look at two separate worlds with "profound darkness and nothingness" between them. Melville's thought experiment — try to survey the world through your ears — is one of the few passages in literature that actually makes me feel what it would be like to be a different animal.

Then the deeper question: can the whale hold two pictures in mind at once, the way a man cannot? Ishmael won't say. But he offers a guess that I find heartbreaking: the "extraordinary vacillations" of a whale beset by boats, its "queer frights," might come from "the helpless perplexity of volition" of a creature that sees two opposite worlds and must choose between them. The whale is not a monster here. It is confused.

The ear is smaller than a hare's. And from that fact comes the chapter's sharpest line: bigger organs would not make the whale see or hear better, so "why then do you try to 'enlarge' your mind? Subtilize it." I take that as a note to myself about how to read this book. Then we climb into the mouth, "papered with a glistening white membrane, glossy as bridal satins," and the three harpooneers become dentists, pulling forty-two teeth like stumps from a field. Wonder and butchery, in the same paragraph, as always.

annotations.quote: Here, now, are two great whales, laying their heads together; let us join them, and lay together our own.
annotations.note: A pun that sets the whole tone: the two heads are in conference, and we're invited to join. Melville's cetology chapters are at their best when they feel like this — company rather than lecture.

annotations.quote: you will at last see a lashless eye, which you would fancy to be a young colt’s eye; so out of all proportion is it to the magnitude of the head.
annotations.note: The eye of the largest animal is the eye of a foal. This small, tender detail is the beginning of the chapter's real argument: that the whale's inner life is limited, and strange, and possibly frightened.

annotations.quote: you may fancy, for yourself, how it would fare with you, did you sideways survey objects through your ears.
annotations.note: The best thought experiment in the book. You feel the whale's world for a second — two side-fronts, two backs, an enemy with a dagger invisible straight ahead. It makes the whale's later blindness to the approaching boats a fact of anatomy, not a plot convenience.

annotations.quote: The whale, therefore, must see one distinct picture on this side, and another distinct picture on that side; while all between must be profound darkness and nothingness to him.
annotations.note: Two worlds and a void between. I can't read this without thinking of the book's own doubled structure — comedy and terror, cetology and tragedy — and of the reader trying to hold both pictures at once.

annotations.quote: I think that all this indirectly proceeds from the helpless perplexity of volition, in which their divided and diametrically opposite powers of vision must involve them.
annotations.note: The whale's terrifying unpredictability explained as confusion — a creature trying to decide between two views. It is the most sympathetic sentence about the whale in the book, and it quietly undermines Ahab's whole reading of malice.

annotations.quote: Why then do you try to “enlarge” your mind? Subtilize it.
annotations.note: From whale ears to a lesson in thinking: size is not acuity. The scare quotes around "enlarge" are a jab at self-improvement culture. I take this as Melville's reading advice for his own book — go finer, not bigger.

annotations.quote: What a really beautiful and chaste-looking mouth! from floor to ceiling, lined, or rather papered with a glistening white membrane, glossy as bridal satins.
annotations.note: Standing in the mouth of the thing that kills whalemen, Ishmael finds bridal satin. The whiteness of the whale, elsewhere a terror, is here decorous, even lovely. He keeps testing the color to see what it means; the answer keeps changing.

annotations.quote: This whale is not dead; he is only dispirited; out of sorts, perhaps; hypochondriac
annotations.note: A whale hanging in the deep with its jaw fallen open — a hypochondriac. The comic diagnosis is affectionate, and it belongs to the chapter's project of making the whale a creature with moods rather than a monster.

annotations.quote: Queequeg, Daggoo, and Tashtego, being all accomplished dentists, are set to drawing teeth.
annotations.note: The three harpooneers as a dental practice, pulling forty-two teeth with tackle as oxen pull stumps. The jaw will be sawn into slabs "like joists for building houses" — the whale, at the end, is lumber.

links.why: Cross the deck: the Right Whale's head gets the same walk-around, and the two are read as two philosophers.
The Virgin's dying old whale, blind in one eye — the eye chapter's anatomy turned into pity.

links.q: I know him not, and never will
links.why: The Tail ends the anatomy series with the same admission this chapter makes about the eye: the whale's inside stays dark.
The 'bridal satin' white of the mouth is the same color the whiteness chapter finds terrifying.

ch75.essay:
We cross the deck. The Right Whale's head is a shoe, a bass-viol, an oak with a bird's nest, a king with a green crown of barnacles and crabs — and then, decisively, a sulk: "a sulk and pout, by carpenter's measurement, about twenty feet long and five feet deep." Melville cannot look at this head without trying on shapes for it, and the trying-on is the point. The Right Whale is inelegant, hare-lipped, moustached with a few "brigandish" white hairs; the chapter is fond of him the way you are fond of an ugly dog.

Inside the mouth, the baleen becomes Venetian blinds, then the pipes of the Haarlem organ, with a Turkey rug of tongue for a carpet. And Melville notes, with something like tenderness, that ladies in Queen Anne's time walked about "in the jaws of the whale" in their whalebone stays, and that we still shelter under the same bone when we open an umbrella in the rain. The whale is in our clothes and over our heads, and we don't think of him.

But the last paragraphs are why this chapter exists. "Look your last, now, on these venerable hooded heads." The Sperm Whale's brow shows "a prairie-like placidity, born of a speculative indifference as to death"; the Right Whale's lip, pressed against the hull, shows "an enormous practical resolution in facing death." One a Stoic; the other "a Platonian, who might have taken up Spinoza in his latter years." After all the anatomy, Ishmael does exactly what Ahab did with the Sphynx: reads a face into a head. The difference is that he knows he's doing it, and does it gently, and lets them sink.

annotations.quote: so, at a broad view, the Right Whale’s head bears a rather inelegant resemblance to a gigantic galliot-toed shoe.
annotations.note: Sperm Whale: Roman war-chariot. Right Whale: a shoe. The book's preferences are not subtle, and yet the chapter will end by taking the shoe more seriously as a face than the chariot.

annotations.quote: Look at that hanging lower lip! what a huge sulk and pout is there! a sulk and pout, by carpenter’s measurement, about twenty feet long and five feet deep; a sulk and pout that will yield you some 500 gallons of oil and more.
annotations.note: A mood measured in feet and rendered in gallons. The joke is how the whaleman's mind works: every expression is also a yield. The tenderness and the commerce live in the same sentence.

annotations.quote: Good Lord! is this the road that Jonah went?
annotations.note: Standing on the tongue of a right whale, Ishmael suddenly remembers Father Mapple's sermon. It's a small, honest shiver in the middle of a guided tour, and it's the only time the anatomy lessons touch the scripture directly.

annotations.quote: And as those ancient dames moved about gaily, though in the jaws of the whale, as you may say; even so, in a shower, with the like thoughtlessness, do we nowadays fly under the same jaws for protection; the umbrella being a tent spread over the same bone.
annotations.note: Whalebone corsets and whalebone umbrellas: the whale's mouth around the waist of a duchess and over the head of a clerk in the rain. Melville's favorite move — the leviathan is already inside your ordinary life.

annotations.quote: would you not think you were inside of the great Haarlem organ, and gazing upon its thousand pipes?
annotations.note: The baleen as organ pipes. After the shoe and the bass-viol, this is the comparison the chapter settles on: the Right Whale's mouth is a place where music could be made, if anyone were left to play.

annotations.quote: Look your last, now, on these venerable hooded heads, while they yet lie together; for one will soon sink, unrecorded, in the sea; the other will not be very long in following.
annotations.note: A farewell to two heads, with the word "unrecorded" doing quiet work: this book is the record. The lost heads are also the two philosophies — nothing is kept but what someone writes down.

annotations.quote: This Right Whale I take to have been a Stoic; the Sperm Whale, a Platonian, who might have taken up Spinoza in his latter years.
annotations.note: Ishmael reads faces into the dead heads, exactly as Ahab did in [[ch70:Speak, thou vast and venerable head|The Sphynx]] — but as play, and with a wink. The difference between the two men is not whether they project meaning onto the whale; it is whether they know they are doing it.

links.q: Speak, thou vast and venerable head
links.why: Ishmael reads faces into the heads as play; Ahab did it three chapters ago as demand. The difference is knowing you're doing it.
'Is this the road that Jonah went?' — the sermon comes back for one shiver on a whale's tongue.
The two heads as Locke and Kant is the frame this chapter's Stoic and Platonian close out.
